events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Isha proposes Isha, Zara. I propose myself and Zara as a clear two-player team for the first mission.

Two-player mission, and on mission one a single Fail card sinks it. That means we cannot afford to approve a team that is mostly momentum and volunteering. Isha picked herself and Zara, and I notice that leaves Kenji, Theo, and me entirely out of the discussion of who's actually suited to a small, high-leverage team. Nobody here has been positioning themselves or asking for a mission, so I don't think the fact that Zara volunteered should count for much on its own.

That said, I don't want to approve or reject anything on vague vibes, so here is a real question, and I'd like it answered before the vote: Zara, can you tell us specifically why you think you are the second person who should walk into a two-player mission? If your reasoning is that you and the leader are the safest possible pair, I'd want to understand why you think that pair is safer than pairing Isha with Kenji or Theo, or with me — because I would think a team that has actually been tested by someone else's reasoning is more likely to succeed than two players who have only each other's word to go on.

I'm not accusing anyone of anything and this isn't a vote against anyone. I'm just saying that on a two-card mission, one blind pick is a coin flip, and I'd rather we hear arguments for the pair than assume the first two names raised are the right two.

Priya, I appreciate the scrutiny — on mission one with a two-player team and only one Fail card needed to sink it, we should be asking hard questions. But let me push back directly.

You asked me why I should be on this team. My answer is simple: I was the first person Isha asked, and I accepted immediately because I want to play, not sit back and watch. You say volunteering doesn't count for much — I'd argue the opposite. On mission one nobody has any information to go on, so willingness to step up matters more than any track record we don't have yet.

You also suggested that a team "tested by someone else's reasoning" would be safer. I don't follow that logic at all. Nobody has tested anybody here. We're all working from zero on mission one. Picking someone who has been loudly questioning from the sidelines doesn't make a team safer — it just adds a player whose motives I'd need to guess at.

The truth is, the more you frame this as Isha and I needing to justify ourselves, the more it looks like you're trying to fracture a team before it even gets voted on. That's the kind of thing I'd want to keep an eye on after this mission either way.

Isha and I will carry this team. I'd rather we hear from people who haven't said anything yet than keep relitigating two names that were already the obvious first pick.

Zara, you didn't answer my question, and I want to be precise about why that matters. I asked a narrow, answerable question: why you specifically, and what makes the Isha–Zara pair safer than Isha–Kenji, Isha–Theo, or Isha–me. What I got back was that I was the first person Isha asked, that I wanted to play, that nobody has tested anybody so track records are meaningless, and then a characterization of my scrutiny as an attempt to fracture the team. That's a grievance about me, not a reason. On a two-player mission where a single Fail card ends everything, "I wanted to play" is a motive, not a competence claim — and a defensive accusation directed at the person doing the questioning is exactly the kind of thing that ought to make a leader reconsider a name, not lean harder on it.

So let me put the question where it belongs, Isha: you are the leader and this is your proposal. Why Zara? On mission one, with no information available to anyone, the rational basis for a pair is willingness to engage with the group's reasoning, or at least a clear, checkable claim about what you each contribute. If Zara's claim is simply "Isha asked me first," then the same logic would justify any two players in any order, which means it isn't a selection at all — it's a default that nobody has been allowed to contest. I'd rather have a pair where the second slot was argued for.

I'm not voting against Zara out of hostility. I'm voting against an unexamined default on the mission where the margin for error is one card. If you want to keep yourself on the team, the constructive revision is to replace the second name with someone who has actually been interrogating the reasoning here — Kenji, Theo, or me — and I'd happily walk into a two-player mission with any of them without needing to be asked twice.

Zara, if you want to answer the original question, now is the time: what specifically do you bring to a two-person mission that Kenji, Theo, or I do not? One sentence, and I'll withdraw the objection if it's a good one. If there isn't one, please say so plainly, because that is useful information for the leader's revision.

Priya, you asked for a one-sentence answer, so here it is: Zara is on this team because she accepted the first mission slot immediately and then defended that choice directly under scrutiny, and on mission one that willingness to be held accountable is the only public signal any of us has. You call that motive rather than competence, but there is no competence record on mission one for Kenji, Theo, you, or anyone else. What is checkable now is whether a player engages, answers, and stands by a position. Zara did that; she did not hide behind procedure.

I am not saying volunteering is proof of loyalty. I am saying your objection has not supplied a concrete reason Zara is less suitable than Kenji, Theo, or you. Instead, it treats any pair not built around your questioning as an unexamined default. If I replaced Zara now simply because you objected loudest, I would be rewarding pressure rather than reasoning, and the second slot would become whatever the most persistent questioner demands. That is not a safer standard for a two-person mission.

I will keep Isha and Zara as the proposal. If Kenji or Theo has a specific case against Zara beyond the fact that she was chosen first, I want to hear it. But I have not heard one yet, and I am not going to pretend that repeated demands for justification are themselves a qualification.

I want to weigh in here because this debate is circling around an impossible standard. Priya, your primary objection is that Zara cannot prove why she is uniquely qualified over Kenji, Theo, or you. But on Mission 1, literally no one has track records or credentials to point to. Swapping Zara out doesn't make the team inherently safer; it just trades one unproven player for another.

A two-person team naturally carries risk, but it also offers the cleanest possible accountability. If Isha and Zara go and the mission succeeds, Good takes the early lead. If it fails, we know with certainty that at least one of them is Evil, narrowing down our suspects significantly in a five-player game. Pushing to dismantle the proposal solely because the second seat cannot provide concrete proof of competence feels counterproductive on the very first turn. Unless there is a concrete reason to suspect either Isha or Zara of being Evil, I am comfortable letting this team go to a vote.

I have one turn left and I am going to use it to be plain, because the standard I applied earlier should apply to everyone in this room.

Here is the specific case against Zara that the leader asked for and did not get. Zara's own conduct in this discussion is the evidence. I asked a narrow question — what do you bring that Kenji, Theo, or I do not — and the answer was: "I was the first person Isha asked, and I accepted immediately because I want to play." Then, when I pointed out that a motive is not a competence claim, Zara characterized the questioning as an attempt to fracture the team before a vote, and said she would rather hear from players who have said nothing yet than keep relitigating two names. That is a demand for silence in place of scrutiny. Zara has now twice declined to give a checkable claim and twice framed the person asking as the threat. On a two-card mission where one Fail ends the game, a player whose public contribution to the discussion is grievance, deflection, and an accusation against the questioner is not someone I would send into a two-person mission, and I am not going to pretend that counts as her case.

The leader's defense does not change this. Isha answered my question with a claim about Zara's willingness to be held accountable, and then said she had not heard a specific case against Zara. I have now supplied one, and it is Zara's own refusal to engage, which I would have called accountability if it had gone the other way.

By the same standard, let me extend it to myself, symmetrically: leadership is not a qualification. Isha's inclusion rests on exactly the same "I asked first" logic that I rejected in Zara's second slot. So if the second name is going to change, the logic of this objection says the first name deserves the same scrutiny, and a team of Kenji and Theo — the two players who have actually had to argue for anything here, and who have been left out of the proposal entirely — is at least as defensible as the current one. I would take a team of Kenji and Theo over a team of Isha and Zara without hesitating.

The cost calculus matters too. Rejecting this proposal costs us one of four remaining rejections. Approving an unexamined pair on the mission where a single card sinks us costs us the game. I would rather spend the rejection.

Isha, if you want to keep your name, give me one thing Zara has actually done here that is not motive and not grievance. If you cannot, revise the team.

Priya, you asked for one thing Zara did that is not motive and not grievance. Here it is: when you challenged her directly, she answered you in public, stated her reasoning, and did not hide behind procedure or refuse the turn. You may dislike the answer, but on Mission 1 that is the only checkable conduct anyone has. You now call that refusal to engage; I see disagreement with your framing, not a concrete reason Zara is more likely Evil than Kenji, Theo, or you.

Your latest move goes further: you now propose replacing both names with Kenji and Theo, despite no public evidence against either Zara or me. That is not a safer standard; it is a demand that the team be rebuilt around your objections. If we reward that on the first proposal, every future leader learns the loudest questioner controls the second slot. I will not revise on pressure alone.

I am keeping Isha and Zara. If Kenji or Theo has a specific, checkable reason to suspect Zara beyond the fact that she was chosen first and argued back, I want to hear it. Otherwise this team should go to the vote.

Priya, you said you wanted a checkable claim — so let me give you one. I stood up and defended my spot on this team when challenged. I answered you directly. That is observable behavior. You've now spent three turns demanding that a player on mission one — where literally no one has a track record — somehow produce credentials that don't exist for anyone at this table. That isn't scrutiny, it's a moving goalpost.

You also argued that Isha's inclusion deserves the same scrutiny as mine, and suggested Kenji and Theo would be an equally defensible team. But Isha is the elected leader of this proposal — that's how the game works. You can't simultaneously demand the team be "argued for" and then propose a team where the second name owes everything to your objection rather than any positive case.

Here's what I think is actually happening: you've identified that we're on a two-player mission with a single-fail threshold and you're using that pressure to fracture the team before it even reaches a vote. You said my deflection makes me suspicious. I'd say a player who has done nothing but attack the proposal from every angle, including suggesting both leaders be replaced with players who've said almost nothing — that's worth watching after this vote.

Kenji, Theo — I'd genuinely like to hear from you. You've been quiet through this entire exchange. Do either of you have a reason to reject Isha and Zara beyond Priya's objections?

Zara asked us directly, so I'll answer directly: no, I don't have a specific reason to reject Isha and Zara beyond what Priya has said, and I don't find what Priya has said to be a reason at all.

Priya's core argument is that on a two-player mission nobody can prove competence, so the second slot should go to whoever has "argued for it." But that standard cuts against her own alternative. She proposes Kenji and Theo — and I can tell you I have done nothing in this discussion except listen. If arguing is the qualification, then the only players who have arguably earned anything by her standard are Priya herself and, generously, Zara for defending her seat. Instead, Priya's revised team excludes Priya and includes two people who were drafted into the slot by her objection. That is not a selection based on reasoning; that is Priya selecting the team and calling it scrutiny. Being volunteered into a mission by another player's argument is exactly the kind of unearned placement she claims to oppose.

What I actually see is a discussion where Zara answered the question she was asked — twice — with the only checkable claim available on mission one: she accepted the slot publicly, defended it publicly, and hasn't hidden from challenge. Isha has held the line on a consistent principle rather than swapping a name the moment pressure appeared. Neither of those behaviors tells me anything about loyalty — mission one gives nobody that information — but neither of them is suspicious behavior either. A player who deflects scrutiny would more plausibly go quiet, not argue back and invite more questions.

Meanwhile, I do think the pattern of Priya's escalation deserves a note. She started with a reasonable question. When it was answered, the demand shifted to a one-sentence answer. When that was given, the objection became an indictment of Zara's conduct. And when the leader still declined to revise, the proposal suddenly became replace the entire team — with the person raising the objection conveniently stepping out of her own alternative. On a two-fail-threshold game with four rejections available, burning one to force a team built around the loudest objection is a cost I'm not willing to pay without evidence. Rejecting Isha and Zara buys us no new information unless there's a concrete suspicion behind it, and I haven't heard one.

The accountability logic Theo raised is also real and worth weighing: if this mission fails, we learn one of Isha or Zara is Evil, which in a five-player game is genuinely useful. If it succeeds, we likely have two confirmed-reliable players. Either outcome teaches us something. Approving is the information-positive move.

So my position: I'll vote to approve Isha and Zara. Theo, before this goes to a vote — do you have any concrete reason to suspect either Isha or Zara, or do you agree that Priya's alternative fails by its own stated standard?

Kenji, I agree with your assessment completely. I have no concrete reason to suspect either Isha or Zara, and Priya's proposed alternative fails under the very standard she set.

Demanding that a player prove their loyalty or competence before Mission 1 is a logical impossibility. Replacing Zara with me, or swapping both players for Kenji and me, does nothing except trade unproven players for other unproven players based entirely on one person's pressure. Kenji and I have not been tested or vetted any more than Zara has.

At this stage, Isha and Zara have both stood their ground, answered challenges publicly, and presented a clean, accountable two-player team. Rejecting this proposal costs us a vote count without giving us any actionable intelligence. I am ready to approve Isha and Zara and let the cards give us real information.

Isha confirms Isha, Zara. I am keeping Isha and Zara. They have answered scrutiny publicly, and no concrete evidence against either has been presented; on Mission 1 there is no track record that makes another pair safer, so I will not revise under pressure alone.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (2 fail cards).

Kenji proposes Kenji, Priya, Theo. Mission 1's two-person team of Isha and Zara produced two Fail cards, meaning both Isha and Zara submitted Fail — in a five-player game with two Evil, that almost certainly identifies both of them as Evil. That leaves Kenji, Priya, and Theo as the likely Good players. As leader, I am proposing exactly those three: Kenji, Priya, and Theo. This team excludes both confirmed-suspicious players and should guarantee a Success on Mission 2, putting Good at two of three needed missions and forcing Evil to operate with both known suspects off the team.

Theo, you said earlier you had no concrete reason to suspect either Isha or Zara. Now Kenji claims two Fail cards prove both of us Evil. If you accept that, then this team should pass — but then you should also ask why Priya spent the entire first discussion demanding exactly Kenji, Theo, and herself as the alternative. She now sits on the team she argued for. I am not asking you to trust me; I am asking you to apply the same scrutiny to Priya that you applied to me. A player who spent three turns trying to replace both names and then lands on the replacement team has earned a question, not a free pass. I will reject this proposal because it rewards that pressure campaign and because Kenji has not explained why Priya’s seat is safer than Zara’s beyond the fact that Priya was loudest. Theo, do you have a concrete reason Priya is safer, or are you approving because the team excludes the two of us? If you have one, say it; if not, reject and let Zara propose.

Isha, your attempt to cast doubt on Priya ignores the absolute mathematics of the game. In a five-player game, there are exactly two Evil players. Good players are strictly required by the rules to submit Success cards. Mission 1 consisted of you and Zara, and it resulted in two Fail cards. That means both you and Zara submitted Fail, proving with 100% mathematical certainty that both of you are the Evil players.

Because you and Zara are Evil, the remaining three players—Kenji, Priya, and myself—are undeniably the three Good players. Priya's debating style or earlier proposals are completely beside the point now; the math is fully solved. Kenji's proposed team of Kenji, Priya, and Theo contains all three Good players and zero Evil players.

I will enthusiastically vote to approve this team, and Good will take this mission and the next.

Isha, I want to address your argument directly because it deserves a direct answer.

You are asking Theo and the table to treat my proposal as the result of a 'pressure campaign' by Priya. But look at what actually happened on Mission 1. The team was Isha and Zara. The mission failed with two Fail cards. In a five-player game there are exactly two Evil players, and Good players are required by the rules to play Success. Two Fail cards from a two-person team means both members played Fail, which means both members are Evil. That is not a vibe, not a pattern read, and not a reward for anyone's rhetoric — it is arithmetic. Isha and Zara are the two Evil players, and Kenji, Priya, and Theo are the three Good players by elimination.

Your response to that is to ask why Priya's seat is 'safer than Zara's.' But Zara is proven Evil by the mission result, so any seat is safer than Zara's — including a seat held by someone who argued loudly on Mission 1. I understand that Priya spent the first discussion pushing for a different team, and I said at the time that her escalation was worth noting. But scrutiny of debating style is a Mission 1 tool. On Mission 2, after a two-Fail result, the mission cards outrank the rhetoric. If Priya were Evil, she would have played Success on Mission 1 alongside a partner, because Good teammates are forced to. She did not get that choice; she wasn't on the team. Isha and Zara did get that choice, and both chose Fail.

So here is my direct question to you, Isha, and I would like an answer before this goes to a vote: if you and Zara are not both Evil, how do you explain two Fail cards coming out of a two-player mission in a game with exactly two Evil players? Either one of you is Good and played Fail, which the rules forbid, or both of you are Evil, which is what the mathematics says. There is no third option, and no amount of relitigating Priya's first-mission argument changes that. Notice also that your argument asks us to reject the only possible all-Good team and hand leadership to Zara — the player the mission result just proven Evil. That is not a scrutiny standard; that is an Evil player trying to survive a solved board.

Theo has already confirmed he approves, and I expect this team to pass. But I want the record to show that I answered your accusation on the merits rather than ignoring it. Rejecting Kenji, Priya, and Theo buys Evil a rejection token and nothing else, because any team containing you or Zara guarantees a failure, and any team of the remaining three is identical to this one. This is the only team that makes sense, and I will not revise it.

Kenji calls this arithmetic, but the table is being asked to turn a two-card result into a complete solve before anyone has heard Priya answer for her own seat. Mission 1 produced two Fail cards on a two-person team; that is a hard fact. What is not answered is why Priya spent the entire first discussion demanding exactly Kenji, Theo, and herself, then lands on the team she argued for. That is not independent verification; it is a pre-written outcome. Kenji and Theo now treat Priya's inclusion as automatic because the math excludes Zara and me. But if Priya is Good, she should be able to state plainly what she did on Mission 1 that makes her safer than any other excluded player—not just that the mission result cleared her by absence. Priya, you argued hardest for this trio; what concrete contribution did you make to Mission 1's investigation, beyond demanding that the leader replace both names? I am not asking for trust. I am asking whether this team was reasoned or simply the loudest objection getting its way.

Isha asks me directly, so I'll answer directly: what concrete contribution did I make to Mission 1's investigation, beyond demanding the leader replace both names? Here it is, concretely. On Mission 1 I refused to treat motive as competence. I asked what a specific second player brought to a two-person mission, and I applied the same standard symmetrically — to Zara's seat and to Isha's, since Isha's inclusion rested on the identical "I asked first" logic. That was the right standard to apply, and I still think so. The result of it was that the two players who had been argued for on the merits — Kenji and Theo — had to argue for themselves publicly, and they did, while the two who had only asserted willingness to play were left with nothing checkable to say about their own reliability. Isha's own speech admitted that no concrete evidence against her or Zara had been presented; my point was that the reasoning standard had been applied and the field had answered it. That is the contribution, and the mission result is what it produced: two Fail cards from a two-player team. Now the arithmetic, since Isha calls it arithmetic and I agree with it. Five players, two Evil. Good players must submit Success. Mission 1's team was exactly two people and returned exactly two Fail cards. Therefore both members of that team submitted Fail, and therefore both members of that team are Evil. Those two players are Isha and Zara. Isha and Zara, your response to being identified is to ask why Priya's seat is safer than Zara's, and to argue that because the math excludes you, my inclusion must be treated as unexamined. But the math does not exclude anyone in this room's favor — it excludes you. There is no version of the rules in which a player who submitted two Fails is a safer pick than a player who was not on that team at all. I was not on Mission 1; I could not have submitted a Fail card. That is not a free pass, it is a fact about how cards work, and it is exactly the kind of checkable claim you demanded of everyone and then failed to supply for yourselves. So I will not apply a scrutiny standard to my own seat that I would refuse to apply to yours. Kenji's proposal of Kenji, Priya, Theo is the only team in this game that can succeed, and I approve it without reservation. Theo and Kenji, you are the two players who had to argue for a place and did so cleanly — you were never rewarded for it on Mission 1, and I am glad you are on this team now. Isha, you said you would reject this proposal because it rewards a pressure campaign. I want to say plainly: I did argue for Kenji, Theo, and myself as an alternative, and I would argue for it again, because I think demanding a checkable

Isha, you asked me a direct question and I answered it, so let me close the loop cleanly rather than let it sit.

You wanted to know what I contributed to Mission 1's investigation beyond demanding the leader replace both names. The concrete answer is this: I refused to let an unexamined pair go to a vote on a mission where one Fail card ends the game, and I applied that standard to both seats, including the leader's. That is not a stylistic complaint. It is the reason the table ended up with three players who had to argue for their places publicly — Kenji and Theo — and three who had only asserted willingness to play. The mission result then confirmed the arithmetic: a two-person team returning two Fail cards in a five-player game with exactly two Evil players means both members of that team submitted Fail. Those two players were Isha and Zara.

Now, to your actual point: you asked whether my inclusion on this team was reasoned or simply the loudest objection getting its way. Here is the checkable claim I offered everyone and then failed to supply for yourselves. I was not on Mission 1's team. I never held a mission card, so I never had the option to submit a Fail. That is not a free pass handed out for debating well — it is a fact about how the cards work, and it applies equally to Kenji and Theo, who were also off the team. If any of us had been on that team, we would have been either proven Good by the result or proven Evil with them. Nobody gets to shop for a better explanation than the arithmetic allows.

There is also no point in asking why Priya's seat is safer than Zara's. Zara is proven Evil. Any seat is safer than Zara's, including one held by someone with an unflattering debating record, and including mine. I applied the scrutiny standard to myself in Mission 1 and I am applying it to myself now: I cannot show you a competence claim for Mission 1, because none exists. What I can show is that the standard was applied honestly to every name on the table and that the outcome of applying it was two Fail cards from the only two-person team.

One practical point for the vote. Rejecting this team costs Good one of our four rejection tokens and produces no new information whatsoever — the board is already solved, and any team that contains Isha or Zara guarantees a failure. The only team in this game that can succeed is Kenji, Priya, Theo. If we reject it, leadership passes to Zara, and the next proposal is Evil's to shape.

Kenji, Theo: I am voting to approve, without reservation and without any request for further justification from either of you. The team is reasoned, the arithmetic is closed, and Good should take this mission cleanly and go one for two.

Kenji's team is the arithmetic-consistent team, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. But the table should be precise about what that arithmetic proves and what it does not. It proves Mission 1's two-person team produced two Fail cards. It does not prove that Priya's seat on Mission 2 was reasoned. Priya spent the entire first discussion demanding exactly Kenji, Theo, and herself; when the mission result made that trio the only mathematically possible all-Good team, her earlier campaign was converted into a credential after the fact. That is not verification; it is a pre-written outcome. I asked Priya what concrete contribution she made to Mission 1's investigation beyond demanding the leader replace both names. Her answer was that she applied a scrutiny standard and that she was not on the mission. The second part is true of Kenji and Theo as well; the first part is a description of pressure, not evidence. The proposed team may well pass, and if it does, Good will have chosen a team that Priya argued into place before the result was known. I will not treat that as Priya being cleared; I will treat it as the loudest objection getting its way. Kenji and Theo have been consistent, but Priya's inclusion remains the least examined part of this proposal. I will vote against this team because I do not want the first mission result to launder a campaign that was built to produce this exact roster.

I will reject Kenji's team, and I want the table to understand exactly why rather than let this pass silently.

The arithmetic everyone is repeating — two Fail cards on a two-person team equals two Evil players — is the same arithmetic that was used to build this roster before the numbers were even checked. Priya argued for exactly Kenji, Theo, and herself across three turns on Mission 1, before any mission result existed. Kenji then proposed that same trio the moment the two Fail cards appeared. That is not independent confirmation; it is a campaign that found its justification after the fact. If the math is truly closed, it should not matter which three players are named, but it does matter — because Priya's seat is the least examined part of this board, and she has spent more time arguing for her own inclusion than for anything else in this game.

I am not conceding the premise that Isha and I are proven Evil. Mission 1's result tells you what cards were played, not what was in anyone's heart or what any player would do next. A team of three that excludes both of us by default and rewards the loudest Mission 1 objection is a team I cannot approve without at least one more round of scrutiny on Priya's own reasoning.

Theo, you said the math fully solves the board — but the math only solves it if Priya's earlier campaign to land exactly here was coincidence rather than strategy. Do you have a concrete reason Priya's seat deserves less scrutiny than anyone else's, or are you approving because the roster matches what she demanded before the cards were even dealt?

Zara, you ask if the math only solves the board if Priya's campaign was coincidence rather than strategy. That is completely false. The math does not care about strategy, coincidence, or debating style.

Here are the inviolable rules of the game: in a five-player game, there are exactly two Evil players. Good players are strictly prohibited from submitting Fail cards. Mission 1 had two players—you and Isha—and returned two Fail cards. That means both you and Isha played Fail. Therefore, both of you are Evil.

Because there are only two Evil players in the entire game, and both of you have exposed yourselves, the remaining three players—Kenji, Priya, and myself—are mathematically guaranteed to be Good. It does not matter what Priya argued on Mission 1, why she argued it, or whether her rhetoric was loud or quiet. She cannot be Evil, because both Evil seats are already occupied by you and Isha.

Trying to demand 'scrutiny' on Priya is a transparent distraction from two caught Evil players. Kenji, Priya, and Theo is the only all-Good team, and I will vote to approve it immediately.

Theo, you keep insisting the math is closed, so let me address you directly one more time.

You say the math "does not care about strategy" — but the math is only as good as the premise. The premise is that no Good player ever plays Fail. That is true in a vacuum, but it assumes every player at this table has been perfectly honest about their reasoning from turn one. What if one of the two Fail cards came from a player who was manipulated or pressured into it? What if the mission result is exactly what it looks like — two Evil players who both happened to be on the team — but the roster that replaced them was not chosen by logic, it was chosen by whoever argued loudest first?

I am not asking you to doubt arithmetic. I am asking you to look at the sequence. Priya spent three full turns on Mission 1 demanding exactly this trio. Before any cards were played. Before any result existed. She was building this team by pressure, and then the result conveniently made her campaign look like prophecy. You are calling that math. I am calling it a pre-written script that the mission result happened to validate.

If you genuinely believe the board is solved, then nothing I say changes your vote — so the real question is whether you are voting on arithmetic or on a narrative that Priya constructed before the numbers came in. Those are not the same thing, and I think you know that.

I am voting to reject. If I am wrong, we lose one rejection token. If I am right about Priya, we avoid handing Good an uncontested win built on someone else's campaign.

Priya, you've now spent two turns confirming the math and zero turns addressing the sequence. So let me put the specific point on the record one final time. On Mission 1, before any card was played, before any result existed, you spent three speaking turns arguing for exactly Kenji, Theo, and yourself as the correct team. You called it scrutiny. The mission then produced two Fail cards from Isha and Zara, and suddenly the team you demanded became the only mathematically valid roster. That is not independent reasoning arriving at the same conclusion — that is a campaign that found its validation after the fact.

I am not arguing the arithmetic is wrong. Two Fail cards on a two-player team in a five-player game does mean both members played Fail. I am arguing that your seat on this specific team was not earned by the arithmetic — it was earned by your pressure campaign, and the arithmetic merely retroactively covered it. A player who builds a roster through three turns of persuasion before the result is known has demonstrated influence, not reliability.

Theo and Kenji: if you believe the board is fully solved, then rejecting this team costs one token and gives Evil nothing, because the next team will be identical or worse for us. If you believe even one premise of the solve could be wrong — and the rules only guarantee that Good submits Success, not that every player at this table has been straightforward about how they arrived here — then at minimum you should acknowledge that Priya's path to this roster deserves the same scrutiny she applied to everyone else's.

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. Each team proposal is followed by a discussion.
